articles.title: Turtle Herbivory Suppresses Seagrass Function but Reveals Recovery Potential in a Remote Coral Reef Atoll

articles.title: An integrated GIS and remote-sensing framework for district-level dengue risk assessment in northern India: development of a spatial Dengue Risk Index and assessment of its spatial concordance with reported incidence
paragraphs: Dengue is an increasingly important vector-borne disease driven by climate variability, urbanization, environmental change, and population growth. Despite its rising burden in northern India, district-level spatial epidemiological frameworks integrating environmental suitability, transmission hazard, and population vulnerability remain limited. This study developed an integrated geographic information system (GIS)- and remote-sensing (RS)-based Dengue Risk Index (DRI) describing long-term spatial susceptibility to dengue in Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh, and assessed its spatial concordance with reported dengue incidence.

A GIS-based multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) framework incorporating the analytic hierarchy process (AHP) integrated 14 environmental, topographic, hydrological, and socio-demographic variables into three thematic components: the Environmental Suitability Index (ESI; six variables), Hazard Index (HI; five variables), and Vulnerability Index (VI; three variables). Relative humidity and the Normalized Difference Moisture Index were excluded after redundancy screening. Rainfall was derived from India Meteorological Department (IMD) 0.25° daily gridded data for 2025, elevation from the Copernicus 30 m DEM, and population density from WorldPop 2025 constrained estimates. Standardized (1–5) raster layers were integrated using the Weighted Linear Combination (WLC) approach to construct the DRI. Spatial concordance between block-level mean DRI and laboratory-confirmed dengue incidence in 2025 (225 cases, 20 blocks) was assessed using Pearson’s and Spearman’s correlation, linear and negative binomial regression, influence diagnostics, and global Moran’s I with Lagrange multiplier tests for spatial dependence.

The DRI (1–5 relative scale) showed marked spatial heterogeneity, with higher values in the central and western parts of the district. Chargawan, which contains Gorakhpur city, was the only block classified as Very High risk, followed by Sahjanwa, Piprauli, and Jungle Kaudia (High), whereas Brahmpur was classified as Very Low risk. Overall, 32.87% of the district (1,090.2 km2) was classified as High or Very High risk. The single very high-risk block accounted for 48.9% of reported cases. However, concordance between block-level DRI and incidence was weak and not statistically significant (Pearson's r = 0.16, p = 0.49; Spearman's ρ = −0.003, p = 0.99; R2 = 0.03; incidence rate ratio per 0.1 DRI = 1.05, 95% CI 0.91–1.21). Neither incidence nor the regression residuals showed significant spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I = −0.13 and −0.17; p ≥ 0.44), so spatial regression was not required.

The DRI provides a transparent, reproducible description of long-term spatial susceptibility to dengue that integrates environmental suitability, transmission hazard, and population vulnerability. Because its concordance with single-year, block-level incidence was weak and non-significant, it should not be interpreted as a predictor of dengue incidence or as a validated risk model. The framework may help district programs structure surveillance planning, but multi-year incidence, finer spatial units, and entomological data are needed before it is used to allocate interventions.

articles.title: Analytical Approaches for Detection, Characterization, and Environmental Significance of Suspended Particulate Matter in Aquatic Systems: A Scoping Review
paragraphs: Suspended particulate matter (SPM) represents a component of aquatic systems, acting both as a carrier of contaminants and as a factor shaping ecosystem functioning. This review summarizes recent progress in methods for detecting and quantifying SPM in natural waters. Traditional gravimetric analysis provides a direct mass‐based reference, while optical approaches such as turbidimetry and nephelometry enable rapid and automated assessments. Granulometric techniques, including sedimentation and laser diffraction, contribute to understanding particle size distribution and its role in transport, settling, and pollutant interactions. Chemical characterization, based on spectroscopic and spectrometric methods, identifies the composition of SPM and its association with heavy metals, organic pollutants, and microplastics. Particular attention is given to the ecological risks posed by fine particles, which remain suspended longer and enhance contaminant mobility. The review integrates findings from hydrochemistry, analytical chemistry, and environmental monitoring, outlining both the strengths and limitations of existing methods and highlighting directions for improving water‐quality assessment and ecological risk evaluation.

articles.title: Inkjet and Related Printing Technologies for Plant Systems: From Physiological Monitoring to Functional Biofabrication
paragraphs: Featuring non-contact, high-precision, and multi-material deposition, inkjet and related printing technologies offer a new alternative technique for plant systems. However, the spatial heterogeneity, continuous growth, and sensitivity of plant tissues to external perturbations make it difficult for conventional methods to target specific sites on living organs. This review evaluates thermal and piezoelectric inkjet printing, together with aerosol jet and electrohydrodynamic printing for plant applications. Moreover, it relates the jetting behavior of the printhead to interfacial processes between droplets and plant surfaces. Practical performance is assessed across four dimensions: effective feature size, organ-scale throughput, potential biological damage, and the physiological compatibility of printing inks with plants. Applications are then organized within a framework comprising five tiers: monitoring, delivery, sensing, biofabrication, and intelligent systems. Specifically, recent studies have demonstrated that these printing approaches can be employed for surface labeling and growth tracking of plant organs, localized delivery of agricultural inputs, fabrication of flexible sensors, and construction of living materials (e.g., plant cells). Combined with artificial intelligence technology, these capabilities could form a closed-loop system spanning sensing to feedback, with printing as the precision actuator, potentially shifting plant management from passive observation to active regulation. Finally, this review discusses the challenges of living-interface dynamics, ink biocompatibility, multiscale integration, and data intelligence. It further outlines the prospects of these technologies for programmable plants and living agricultural interfaces. By bridging printing technologies, plant systems, and functional biofabrication, this review provides a unified framework to guide the development of intelligent and sustainable agricultural systems.

paragraphs: Escherichia coli (E. coli) has developed resistance to multiple antibiotic classes, complicating treatment in both human and veterinary medicine. articles.title: Differential Impacts of Anthropogenic Disturbance on Community Composition and Alpha Diversity of Macroinvertebrates at a Large Urban River System
paragraphs: Macroinvertebrates play critical roles in aquatic ecosystems, yet the effects of anthropogenic land‐use disturbance on macroinvertebrate communities and their taxonomic and functional diversity remain poorly understood, particularly in rapidly urbanizing regions of eastern China. Here, we identified 211 macroinvertibrates species from 385 river sites in Ningbo, Zhejiang Province, China. We classified sites as low‐disturbance (LD) or high‐disturbance (HD) based on surrounding land use. This study examined differences in macroinvertebrate community composition, taxonomic and functional diversity, and functional feeding groups (FFGs) between disturbance levels, and further explored the potential direct and indirect effects of land use and environmental factors using structural equation modeling (SEM). Macroinvertebrate community composition differed significantly (p = 0.001) between LD and HD sites, with HD sites showing lower taxonomic and functional diversity. The relative abundance of FFGs also shifted with disturbance level, with filterers, gatherers, and predators more abundant at LD sites, whereas scrapers and shredders increased at HD sites. SEM further indicated that agricultural and urban land uses were negatively associated with both taxonomic and functional diversity, while non‐purgeable organic carbon (NPOC) showed a positive association with diversity. These findings demonstrate that anthropogenic land‐use disturbance can restructure macroinvertebrate communities and reduce multiple dimensions of biodiversity, highlighting the importance of integrating both taxonomic and functional information into ecological assessments of human‐dominated river systems.

articles.title: Fungus above us: exploring the atmospheric mycobiome by aircraft
paragraphs: Fungi play a key role in ecosystems, influencing the global bioaerosol budget and pollution dynamics even when metabolically inactive. Despite this, diversity and transport of fungi in the atmosphere are not well explored. This study shows that the atmosphere contains diverse fungi with varied ecological classifications and recruitment patterns reflecting underlying terrestrial habitats. Abundant genera include Neoascochyta, Cladosporium, Alternaria, Coniothyrium, Penicillium, Hymenochaetopsis, Lachnum, and Fonsecazyma. The atmospheric mycobiome is dominated by decomposers and pathogens; over 40% of the sampled airborne fungi are putative plant or animal pathogens. Using aircraft surveys from 2022 to 2023 in distinct seasons alongside comprehensive environmental datasets, airborne fungal diversity was found to decline with altitude and increasing vegetation productivity. Patterns of diversity in atmospheric fungal communities are shaped by vegetation productivity and meteorology. Remote sensing and meteorological data provide valuable insight into this diversity and reinforce the role of local or regional phenology as an important determinant of atmospheric biodiversity. Additionally, the proportional composition of functional guilds in the atmosphere shifts with vegetation productivity and surface winds, suggesting that seasonal transport dynamics may contribute to shaping assembly of the atmospheric mycobiome. This work demonstrates how integrated genomic and environmental datasets acquired by aircraft and satellite data could be leveraged in future to clarify aerobiology questions and contribute to a unified view of fungal ecology.

articles.title: Wolf Predation Likely Eliminated a Beaver Colony in a Drought‐Stressed Pond
paragraphs: Wolves and beavers increasingly co‐occur across the Northern Hemisphere, yet direct observations of their interactions remain rare, and little is known about how beavers respond behaviourally to predation risk under natural conditions. On 29 December 2024, a wolf killed an adult beaver on a foraging trail in Białowieża Forest, Poland, among the first video‐documented wolf–beaver predation events in Europe. Over the 53‐day monitoring period prior to the predation event, wolves visited the trail on 4 days, while beavers were active on 33 of those days (62%), averaging 4.9 detections per day (7.9 on days with activity). This contrasts with experimental work showing that predator cues alone are often enough to sharply suppress beaver activity. The predation occurred during hydrological drought. The watercourse above and below the pond was nearly dry, likely leaving the colony with nowhere safer to go. We interpret this apparent risk tolerance as consistent with the risk allocation hypothesis, where prey with no low‐risk foraging options cannot sustain antipredator behaviour without compromising essential foraging. Following the predation, the pond remained abandoned for at least 18 months. This expands on a previous report of ponds becoming inactive following wolves predating on dispersing beavers, suggesting predation can also displace established colonies, with potentially cascading consequences for water retention, nutrient cycling and vegetation dynamics. In drought‐affected landscapes, wolf predation could plausibly act as a spatial filter, disproportionately removing these ecosystem engineers from suboptimal habitats. This is a hypothesis that warrants future testing. As droughts intensify under climate change, this could compound into a feedback loop. Fewer active beaver sites would mean less landscape‐scale water retention, deepening drought and further constraining the beaver habitat that remains, and undermining the ecosystem functions that make beaver recolonisation so ecologically valuable.

articles.title: Regenerating forests around Taï National Park sustain biodiversity despite constrained floristic recovery
paragraphs: Extensive deforestation and disturbance have reshaped forest landscapes in West Africa, including areas surrounding Taï National Park, the largest remaining block of Upper Guinean rainforest. Although many degraded areas are currently undergoing regeneration, the capacity of these secondary forests to recover their biodiversity attributes remains insufficiently assessed within this park. This study quantifies the multidimensional restoration of biodiversity across 125 secondary forest plots and 15 primary forest plots representing 14,731 inventoried individuals in four sectors of the park. Using a Bayesian modelling framework, we estimate recovery trajectories of Shannon diversity, floristic composition, functional traits (wood density, leaf mass per area, seed mass), and conservation-relevant species. The different biodiversity attributes recovered at contrasting rates. Diversity was restored more rapidly (λ = 0.06) than floristic composition (λ = 0.03), and these recovery rates varied according to environmental variables. Among these, the presence of remnant trees showed the highest median on diversity (0.53 ± 0.61) and floristic composition (0.37 ± 0.17), promoting the rapid recovery of both attributes, followed by prior land use, particularly cocoa farming which also positively influenced the recovery of alpha diversity (λ = 0.03) and floristic composition (λ = 0.02). Regarding functional traits, they displayed contrasting dynamics: leaf mass per area (LMA) and seed mass recovered rapidly along successional gradients, whereas wood density followed a more gradual recovery trajectory. From a conservation perspective, although the proportion of IUCN Red List species remained stable along the successional gradient, old-growth indicator species were significantly more abundant in primary forests. To ensure the long-term conservation of biodiversity, protecting both primary and regenerating forests is essential to preserve the ecological resilience of this park.

articles.title: Weak dispersal and landscape size inevitably promote local biodiversity in heterogeneous metacommunities of competing species
paragraphs: We provide a general theoretical explanation for a longstanding result in spatial ecology: weak dispersal among habitat patches promotes local species richness. Using analytical approximations of spatial Lotka–Volterra competition models, we show that local species persistence in heterogeneous landscapes can be expressed as the balance between the total density across patches and the local exclusion rate. We further demonstrate that local multispecies coexistence is governed by the feasibility domain, linking spatial coexistence to a structural property of nonspatial competitive systems. Together, these results explain why weak dispersal increases local species richness and why this effect strengthens with the number of available patches, i.e., landscape size. We test these predictions using numerical simulations and find that the theory breaks down only when both dispersal and competitive interactions are very strong, in which case dispersal has a unimodal effect on coexistence. In contrast, landscape size retains a positive effect on coexistence whenever an effect is detectable. We then apply the theory to long-term data from a natural metacommunity of microcrustaceans. We detect strong competition among species and find no detectable effect of dispersal rate on local coexistence, whereas species co-occurrence increases with local landscape size, as predicted by theory. Together, our results identify how dispersal, interaction strength, and landscape size jointly regulate local species richness in competitive systems.

We study a long-standing question in ecology: why does a small amount of movement between habitats often increase the number of species that can live together locally? Although this pattern has been observed in many natural systems, a general explanation has been difficult to establish for communities containing many competing species. Using a mathematical model of species competition across connected habitats, we show that local coexistence depends on a simple balance between two forces. Species are more likely to persist in a habitat when they are abundant across the broader landscape and less likely to persist when strong competition would otherwise drive them locally extinct. This balance allows us to predict when dispersal among habitats promotes biodiversity and when it does not. We also show that the chance that all species coexist locally is closely linked to existing ecological theory developed for isolated communities. We test these predictions using computer simulations and long-term observations of microcrustaceans living in Finnish rock pools. We find strong agreement between theory and data, but also reveal the ecological situations in which it breaks down. Our results provide a unified framework linking dispersal, competition, landscape size, and biodiversity across spatially connected ecosystems.

articles.title: PoLoCo: a reproducible pooled low-coverage workflow for draft genome assembly and allele frequency analysis from ethanol-preserved small non-model invertebrates
paragraphs: Many ecologically important small invertebrates are preserved in ethanol, which compromises DNA integrity and severely limits their potential to be utilized in further genomic research. The lack of soil arthropod representation ultimately results in limited availability of reference genomes and population genomic inference from pooled sequencing (Pool-seq).

We introduce PoLoCo (Pooled Low-Coverage), a reproducible workflow integrating pooled specimen draft genome assembly from ethanol-preserved specimens with population-level allele-frequency analysis. We assembled a 411 Mb draft genome of Entomobrya nivalis from pooled short reads, achieving 97.7% BUSCO completeness despite notable fragmentation. Comparison with the published reference genome showed partial genomic correspondence while also revealing reference-dependent differences in the retained SNP datasets. The application of PoLoCo to 82 retained pooled populations produced a final distance-thinned allele-frequency dataset suitable for population-scale genomic inference. Case-study execution documented the computational requirements of the major workflow components on standard HPC infrastructure, with the workflow, documentation, and software environments openly available in Zenodo.

PoLoCo demonstrates that draft genome assemblies and reproducible Pool-seq allele-frequency analyses can be performed with long-preserved sample material from the field. PoLoCo integrates reference construction, sync-based allele-frequency analysis, and benchmarking into a free and open workflow. It establishes a reproducibility benchmark for biodiversity genomics and yields a transferable workflow for ecological and evolutionary initiatives where high-quality DNA or long-read sequencing is not feasible.

articles.title: An NB-IoT-Based Architecture with Spatial-Statistical Analytics for Cross-Domain Air and Water Quality Monitoring in Aquaculture and Aquatic Environments
paragraphs: The rapid expansion of smart agriculture and precision aquaculture necessitates continuous, high-resolution environmental monitoring to optimize ecosystem stability and prevent catastrophic biomass loss. Conventional Internet of Things (IoT) solutions routinely treat atmospheric and aquatic parameters as isolated domains, neglecting the dynamic physicochemical coupling occurring across the air–water boundary layer. To overcome this domain fragmentation, this study presents an integrated edge-cloud telemetry architecture designed for concurrent, multi-domain environmental monitoring and cross-domain spatial-statistical analysis. The proposed framework employs low-cost, multi-sensor edge nodes integrated with Narrowband IoT (NB-IoT) cellular communication, achieving high signal penetration, energy-efficient operation, and direct base-station connectivity without local gateway dependencies. The system continuously acquires atmospheric parameters (temperature, relative humidity, particulate matter PM1.0/PM2.5/PM10, ozone O3, total volatile organic compounds TVOC, equivalent CO2, Air Quality Index AQI, and Ultraviolet Index UVI) alongside aquatic indicators (water temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen DO, electrical conductivity EC, and turbidity). Telemetry is streamed via Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) to a centralized MySQL cloud database, providing real-time Grafana dashboards, spatial Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) mapping, and automated multi-channel alerting via LINE Notify and email. The architecture was deployed and validated across the Tunghai University aquatic research facility, capturing n = 14,400 synchronized 1-min observations (with an initial raw Packet Delivery Rate of 99.24%). Statistical evaluations accounting for temporal autocorrelation (Neff≈892) and False Discovery Rate correction revealed significant cross-domain associations (padj<0.001), notably an inverse association (r=−0.782, ρ=−0.794, τ=−0.612) between ambient air temperature and aquatic dissolved oxygen physically consistent with Henry’s Law of gas solubility, an inverse association (r=−0.763) between atmospheric humidity and dissolved oxygen, and a positive association (r=+0.789, ρ=+0.812) between humidity and aquatic turbidity. First-order partial correlation analysis (rTa,DO∣Tw=−0.172) confirmed that water temperature serves as the primary thermal mediator of dissolved oxygen depletion. By synergizing low-power NB-IoT telemetry with robust multi-domain analytics, this work provides a scalable, empirical foundation for transitioning from reactive threshold alerting to proactive predictive management in precision aquaculture.

questions.modelAnswer:
Reference evidence — final abstract paragraph (verbatim):

The rapid expansion of smart agriculture and precision aquaculture necessitates continuous, high-resolution environmental monitoring to optimize ecosystem stability and prevent catastrophic biomass loss. Conventional Internet of Things (IoT) solutions routinely treat atmospheric and aquatic parameters as isolated domains, neglecting the dynamic physicochemical coupling occurring across the air–water boundary layer. To overcome this domain fragmentation, this study presents an integrated edge-cloud telemetry architecture designed for concurrent, multi-domain environmental monitoring and cross-domain spatial-statistical analysis. The proposed framework employs low-cost, multi-sensor edge nodes integrated with Narrowband IoT (NB-IoT) cellular communication, achieving high signal penetration, energy-efficient operation, and direct base-station connectivity without local gateway dependencies. The system continuously acquires atmospheric parameters (temperature, relative humidity, particulate matter PM1.0/PM2.5/PM10, ozone O3, total volatile organic compounds TVOC, equivalent CO2, Air Quality Index AQI, and Ultraviolet Index UVI) alongside aquatic indicators (water temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen DO, electrical conductivity EC, and turbidity). Telemetry is streamed via Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) to a centralized MySQL cloud database, providing real-time Grafana dashboards, spatial Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) mapping, and automated multi-channel alerting via LINE Notify and email. The architecture was deployed and validated across the Tunghai University aquatic research facility, capturing n = 14,400 synchronized 1-min observations (with an initial raw Packet Delivery Rate of 99.24%). Statistical evaluations accounting for temporal autocorrelation (Neff≈892) and False Discovery Rate correction revealed significant cross-domain associations (padj<0.001), notably an inverse association (r=−0.782, ρ=−0.794, τ=−0.612) between ambient air temperature and aquatic dissolved oxygen physically consistent with Henry’s Law of gas solubility, an inverse association (r=−0.763) between atmospheric humidity and dissolved oxygen, and a positive association (r=+0.789, ρ=+0.812) between humidity and aquatic turbidity. First-order partial correlation analysis (rTa,DO∣Tw=−0.172) confirmed that water temperature serves as the primary thermal mediator of dissolved oxygen depletion. By synergizing low-power NB-IoT telemetry with robust multi-domain analytics, this work provides a scalable, empirical foundation for transitioning from reactive threshold alerting to proactive predictive management in precision aquaculture.
